## Methods

Ethical statement
All animal experiments were conducted in accordance with the ARRIVE guidelines and were approved by the Experimental Animal Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine (Approval Nos. 2024-147 and 2025-112). This study complied with all relevant ethical regulations.

Dataset acquisition and data processing
The datasets GSE113619, GSE178411, GSE53986, GSE241132, and GSE186527 were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/). Notably, GSE283228 and GSE309507 represent RNA sequencing data generated by our institution and have been deposited in GEO. Data processing, including identifier conversion, log₂ transformation for normalization, and extraction of TAM receptor/ligand expression matrices, was processed by R software (v4.3.0). Heatmaps and bar plots were generated to visualize expression patterns by GraphPad Prism (v9.0).

Single-cell RNA sequencing data from human (GSE241132) and murine (GSE186527) skin wound healing studies were analyzed using Seurat (v5.3.0). After initial quality control to retain cells with more than 300 genes and less than 20% mitochondrial reads, potential doublets were identified and removed using DoubletFinder (v2.0.6). The data were normalized, and the top 3000 highly variable genes were selected using the vst method. Batch effects were corrected using Harmony (v1.2.3) integration with orig.ident as the batch covariate. Cells were clustered at a resolution of 0.5 using the first 15 Harmony dimensions. Dimensionality reduction and visualization were performed with UMAP (v0.2.10.0) based on the same Harmony components. Cell types were annotated through a marker-based identification process. Cluster-specific marker genes were identified using the FindAllMarkers function (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, only positive markers, logFC threshold > 0.25, and adjusted p value < 0.05). Cluster identities were assigned based on canonical cell-type markers.

No ethical approval or patient consent was required as all data were sourced from public repositories.

Isolation of primary bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDM) from mice
Bone marrow was harvested from euthanized 4–8-week-old C57BL/6 mice. Femurs and tibias were disinfected with 75% ethanol, dissected, and flushed with cold medium using a syringe. Cells were filtered through a 70 μm strainer, centrifuged (300×g, 5 min), and treated with Red Blood Cell (RBC) lysis buffer (Invitrogen, #00-4333-57). After washing, cells were cultured in macrophage induction medium (20 ng/mL M-CSF; Meilun Bio, #MA0608). Medium was partially replaced on day 3 and fully refreshed on day 5. Differentiated macrophages were utilized by day 7.

Cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) cytotoxicity assay
Macrophages (BMDM) and fibroblasts (L929 from ATCC, #CCL-1) were seeded in 96-well plates and pre-cultured until reaching approximately 60% confluency. LNP-GAS6 mRNA (0.5–25 μg/mL) was added to the respective wells. After 24 h of incubation, 10 μL CCK-8 reagent (Beyotime, #C0037) was added to each well, followed by a 2-h incubation (dark). Absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader, and bar graphs were generated based on the absorbance values.

Calcein AM/PI staining for cell viability
The viability of fibroblasts or macrophages was assessed using Calcein AM/PI staining (Beyotime, #C1371M). After treatment, the culture medium was aspirated, and cells were gently washed once with PBS. A freshly prepared Calcein AM/PI working solution was added (100 μL per well for a 96-well plate), followed by incubation at 37 °C for 30 min in the dark. Cells were visualized under a fluorescence microscope: live cells exhibited green fluorescence, while dead cells showed red fluorescence. All steps were carried out protected from light.

Histopathological analysis of wounds/scars
Wound/scar tissues from animals were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 h, dehydrated through graded ethanol, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned (4 μm). For H&E staining, sections were dewaxed, stained with hematoxylin (5 min) and eosin (1 min), then mounted. For Masson’s trichrome, sections were incubated in Weigert’s iron hematoxylin (10 min), Biebrich scarlet-acid fuchsin (5 min), and aniline blue (5 min) to visualize collagen. Sirius red staining involved picrosirius red solution (1 h), differentiation in acidified water, and polarization microscopy for collagen typing. All slides were imaged using brightfield/polarized light microscopy.

Immunofluorescence staining
Samples were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100, and blocked with 5% Bovine Serum Albumin (BSA) (1 h, room temperature). Primary antibodies (Cleaved Caspase 3 Polyclonal antibody, Proteintech, #25128-1-AP, 1:200; Rat Monoclonal GAS6 antibody, Abcam, #ab86059, 1:200; EMR1 Polyclonal antibody, Proteintech, #27044-1-AP, 1:200) were incubated overnight at 4 °C. After PBS washes, fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibodies (Goat Anti-Rabbit IgG H&L, Abcam, #ab150077, 1:200; Goat Anti-Mouse IgG H&L, Abcam, #ab150116, 1:200; Fluoro 488 Conjugated AffiniPure Rabbit Anti-Rat, BOSTER, #BA1129, 1:200) were applied (1 h, dark, room temperature). Nuclei were stained with Fluoromount-G™ (Yeasen, #36307ES). Fluorescence signals were captured using a fluorescence microscope.

Transwell migration assay
BMDMs (2×10⁵ cells/insert) in complete medium (10% FBS) were seeded in Transwell (8.0 μm, Corning, #3422) upper chambers. Wound-margin skin samples (1–2 mm³) were pre-equilibrated in complete medium (700 μL/well) for 30 min. Co-culture systems (24 h) were established by positioning inserts above tissue-containing wells13. Migrated cells on lower membranes were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, swab-cleared of non-migratory cells, and stained with crystal violet. Quantification was performed via microscopic imaging.

LNP-mRNA formulation and characterization
GAS6 mRNA was synthesized via in vitro transcription from a linearized plasmid (Yaohai Bio.) using BspQI digestion, followed by phenol-chloroform extraction or magnetic bead purification. The IVT reaction was performed with T7 RNA polymerase, modified nucleotides (including m1ψ-UTP), and either co-transcriptional capping (using cap analog) or enzymatic capping post-IVT (using VCE and 2’-O-methyl-transferase). The resulting mRNA was purified using RNA magnetic beads (N412) and quantified by UV and capillary electrophoresis. The optimized mRNA sequence is provided in the file Supplementary Data 1. IL-4 mRNA and Fluc mRNA were obtained commercially (Yaohai Bio. and Absin Bioscience Inc.). LNP-mRNA were prepared by microfluidic mixing of lipid components (SM102/DSPE-PEG2000/DSPC/Cholesterol, 50:1.5:10:38.5 mol%) with mRNA in citrate buffer (pH 4.0) at a 1:3 volumetric ratio. The N/P ratio for the LNP-mRNA formulation was 6:1. Removal of ethanol and unencapsulated mRNA was performed by dialysis (PBS, 4 °C, 18 h; Slide-A-Lyzer™ 20K MWCO, Thermo Scientific) or ultrafiltration (4 °C, 3000×g, 20 min; UFC805096, Merck-Millipore). Sterilized LNP-mRNA (0.22 μm filtration) was stored at 4 °C. The size, polydispersity index (PDI), and Zeta potential were measured by dynamic light scattering (DLS). The encapsulation efficiency was quantified using the RNA-specific fluorescent dye Quant-iT™ RiboGreen™ (Thermofisher Scientific). Encapsulation efficiency (%) = [(Total mRNA – Free mRNA)/Total mRNA] × 100. The morphology and structure were analyzed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM).

Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
Mouse GAS6 (#E-EL-M0282), IL-6 (#E-EL-M0044), and TNF-α (#E-EL-M3063) ELISA Kit was purchased from Elabscience. For fibroblasts and macrophages, supernatants from LNP-GAS6 mRNA-transfected cells were collected at 24/48/72 h. For skin tissue, the supernatant extracted after lysis was subjected to subsequent testing (POD 1-14). According to the manufacturer’s instructions, standards/samples (100 μL/well) were incubated with capture antibody (90 min, 37 °C), detection antibody (1 h, 37 °C, 3× PBS-T washes), horseradish peroxidase (HRP) conjugate (30 min, 37 °C, 5× PBS-T washes), and substrate solution (15 min, 37 °C) before termination with stop solution. Absorbance at 450 nm was measured and concentrations calculated via standard curve.

Flow cytometry analysis of efferocytosis
BMDMs were seeded in a 12-well plate at a density of 1×10⁵ cells/well. Apoptotic Jurkat T cells were induced by 15-min UV irradiation, followed by 4-h incubation. Apoptotic cells were labeled with Carboxyfluorescein diacetate, succinimidyl ester (CFDA-SE, Beyotime, #C0051) for 15 min, resuspended in fresh medium for 30 min, and washed twice with PBS. Jurkat T cells were resuspended in medium and added to BMDMs (adjusted to a 5:1 ratio of apoptotic cells: BMDMs). Co-cultures were incubated for 2 h to allow efferocytosis. Non-engulfed apoptotic cells were removed by two PBS washes. The remaining cells were harvested and stained with PerCP/Cyanine 5.5 Anti-Mouse F4/80 Antibody (Elabscience, #E-AB-F0995J) on ice for 15 min (dark). After two PBS washes, cells were transferred to flow cytometry tubes. Fluorescence-positive cell percentage and mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) of F4/80⁺/CFDA-SE⁺ populations were quantified using a flow cytometer. Detailed gating strategies for efferocytosis analysis are provided in the Supplementary Information (Supplementary Fig. 4f).

Total RNA extraction and reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR)
Total RNA was extracted and analyzed using commercial kits, reverse-transcribed into cDNA (Hifair® V one-step RT-gDNA digestion SuperMix for qPCR, Yeasen, #11142ES60), and diluted 5–10× before storage at −80 °C. SYBR Green-based qPCR (Hieff® qPCR SYBR Green Master Mix, Yeasen, #11201ES08) was performed with gene-specific primers (Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 1) targeting Gapdh (internal control), Gas6, Nos2, Arg1, Il1b, Il10, Tnf, Csf1, Cxcl12, Ndufa3, Uqcrb, and Cox5a, with relative expression quantified via ΔΔCt method.

Hydrogel preparation and characterization
PLGA-PEG-PLGA hydrogel (MeloPEG, #904330) was thawed (4–6 h, room temperature), dissolved in PBS to 20% (w/v) with periodic stirring (≥3× daily, 5 min/session, 4 °C) until forming transparent colloid. Gelation capacity was tested by mixing hydrogel with LNP/LNP-mRNA (1:1 vol ratio), followed by 37 °C incubation or in vivo application (murine wound). PKH26-labeled LNPs were blended with hydrogel (1:1 vol ratio) for confocal microscopy-based spatial distribution analysis. The hydrogel microstructure and pore size were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and its physical properties were validated on ex vivo mouse skin. LNP-Fluc mRNA was mixed with hydrogel at a 1:1 ratio. After gelation at 37 °C, the LNP-Fluc mRNA@Gel was incubated with PBS, complete medium, esterase (MedChemExpress, #HY-P2831), collagenase I (BioFroxx, #1904GR001), pH 6.5, or 200 μM H₂O₂ in PBS as degradation media. Supernatants were collected at 6, 12, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h for mRNA concentration measurement to calculate the cumulative mRNA release, and the remaining hydrogel mass was weighed to calculate the residual hydrogel ratio. Furthermore, amplitude sweep tests were performed to probe the mechanical integrity of the hydrogel under physiological (PBS, pH 7.4, 37 °C) and pathophysiological (pH 6.5, 200 μM H₂O₂, 37 °C) conditions, recording the storage (G’) and loss (G”) moduli across a strain range of 0.1% to 100% at 1 Hz. For in vivo degradation analysis, LNP-Fluc mRNA@Gel was subcutaneously injected into the dorsal skin of mice. The implants were retrieved at 6, 12, 24, 48, and 72 h, and the residual hydrogel mass was measured to determine the in vivo retention profile.

Application of LNP-Fluc mRNA-loaded hydrogel
Under anesthesia induced by intraperitoneal injection, male C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old) received 6-mm full-thickness circular excisions on the dorsal skin. The wounds were stabilized using silicon rings and covered with 3M™ Tegaderm™ Transparent Film Dressing to inhibit contraction. LNP-Fluc mRNA-loaded hydrogel (50 μg/mL mRNA) was administered into the wound bed through the film using a syringe and allowed to solidify completely for approximately 15 s. Bioluminescence signals were monitored at 6, 12, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h post-application using an In Vivo Imaging System (IVIS) to quantify intensity and spatial distribution.

Biosafety evaluation
Male C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old) were anesthetized and depilated on the dorsal skin. A total of 50 μg/mL LNP-GAS6 mRNA@Gel was administered via subcutaneous multi-point injection. Dorsal hair regrowth was monitored for 30 days. On day 30, skin, visceral organs, and blood samples were collected for histopathological and biochemical analyses, including Masson’s trichrome staining, H&E staining, and ELISA-based detection of inflammatory cytokines.

Transcriptomic sequencing and bioinformatics analysis
Transcriptomic sequencing and bioinformatics analysis were conducted with the support of Shanghai Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd. Full-thickness dorsal wound-edge tissues from mice were harvested at day 3 post-operation, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and homogenized in TRIzol for total RNA extraction. RNA integrity was verified via Agilent 5300 (RQN > 6.5). Stranded mRNA libraries were prepared and sequenced on NovaSeq X Plus. Differential gene expression was analyzed using DESeq2 (FDR < 0.05, |log₂FC| > 1).

ATP concentration assay
BMDMs were lysed directly in culture plates by aspirating the medium and adding 200 μL of ice-cold ATP assay lysis buffer per well (of a 6-well plate). Cells were lysed completely by repeated pipetting. The lysate was centrifuged at 12,000×g for 5 min at 4 °C, and the supernatant was collected. ATP detection working solution (Beyotime, #S0026) was prepared by 1:9 dilution of the reagent. A total of 100 μL working solution was aliquoted into a luminometer plate, incubated at room temperature for 3–5 min, and then mixed with 20 μL of sample or standard. Luminescence (RLU) was measured after a 2-s delay. ATP concentrations were calculated and normalized to protein content (BCA assay).

Animal experiments
For all in vivo wound healing studies, male C57BL/6J mice, female New Zealand White rabbits, and male Bama minipigs were housed under a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle at 22 ± 2 °C and 50 ± 10% humidity. According to previous study, sex has no significant impact on wound repair. A total of 134 male C57BL/6J mice (C57BL/6J Rj substrain; Janvier Labs, France) were used in this study. For all wound healing experiments, male mice aged 6–8 weeks were employed. Mice underwent dorsal full-thickness 6-mm circular excisions under intraperitoneal injection anesthesia, stabilized with silicon rings and 3M Tegaderm film (inhibiting wound contraction). To identify the optimal concentration of LNP-GAS6 mRNA, the treatments were as follows: ⅰ. LNP@Gel, ⅱ. LNP-GAS6 mRNA@Gel (20 μg/ml), ⅲ. LNP-GAS6 mRNA@Gel (50 μg/ml), and ⅳ. LNP-GAS6 mRNA@Gel (80 μg/ml). For the LNP-GAS6 mRNA therapeutic evaluation, the groups included: ⅰ. saline (Ⅰ), ⅱ. Gel (Ⅱ), ⅲ. LNP@Gel (Ⅲ), ⅳ. GAS6 mRNA-LNP@Gel (50 μg/ml) (Ⅳ), ⅴ. recombinant GAS6 protein (10 μg/ml, MedChemExpress) (Ⅴ). Healing parameters (wound area) were tracked at days 0, 3, 7, 10, and 14 post-operation. Peri-wound tissues were harvested at day 3 and underwent immunofluorescence detection of apoptotic cells and Transwell migration assays, while day 30 scar tissues were analyzed via H&E/Masson’s trichrome staining for scar length and collagen architecture. In separate inhibitor studies, RU-301, Bemcentinib, and UNC2025 (MedChemExpress) were applied topically at 50 μg/mL.

A total of 6 female New Zealand White rabbits aged 6–8 months with a body weight of 2.5–3.5 kg were used for the hypertrophic scar model. Four 1-cm-diameter circular full-thickness wounds (ventral surface) per ear, including perichondrium, were surgically excised in rabbits under intravenous anesthesia. These wounds were treated with ⅰ. saline (Ⅰ), ⅱ. Gel (Ⅱ), ⅲ. LNP@Gel (Ⅲ), or ⅳ. LNP-GAS6 mRNA@Gel (50 μg/ml) (Ⅳ) under 3M Tegaderm film. Healing dynamics and hypertrophic scar formation were monitored on days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28, and 60, with collagen organization analyzed via Masson’s trichrome and picrosirius red staining in harvested scar tissues.

A total of 6 male Bama minipigs, aged 12–18 months with a body weight of 20–30 kg, were used for the preclinical wound healing study. Dorsal 15-mm-diameter circular full-thickness excisions were created in Bama minipigs under intramuscular and inhalation anesthesia. These wounds were treated with ⅰ. Gel (Ⅰ), ⅱ. LNP@Gel (Ⅱ), ⅲ. LNP-GAS6 mRNA@Gel (50 μg/ml) (Ⅲ), or ⅳ. h-EGF gel (Ⅳ) under 3M Tegaderm film. The wound healing and scar formation progression were tracked on days 0, 7, 14, 21, 28, and 35, with scar tissues harvested at days 14 and 35, and analyzed via Masson’s trichrome staining for collagen deposition.

Statistical analysis
Data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism (v9.0) or R software (v4.3.0), with ≥3 independent biological replicates per group and representative images illustrated. Normality was verified via Shapiro-Wilk tests. Between-group comparisons employed Student’s t-test (two groups) or one-way/two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post-hoc analysis (≥3 groups). Results were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD).

### Reviewer 2

While the manuscript presents a basic proof-of-concept idea to promoting scarless wound healing through a hydrogel-based mRNA delivery system, the overall study exhibits substantial limitations across multiple critical aspects, including experimental design, material characterization, and mechanistic investigation. These shortcomings are not merely technical or procedural but reflect deeper structural constraints inherent to the material system itself—such as the absence of precise targeting mechanisms, undefined degradation behavior, and limited adaptability to pathological wound environments. In its current form, the work does not provide sufficiently rigorous or convincing evidence to substantiate its proposed therapeutic advantages.
Major Concerns
1. Insufficient Biocompatibility and Safety Evaluation
The study lacks long-term in vivo safety data (e.g., fibrosis scoring, chronic inflammation) to confirm biocompatibility of the hydrogel.
Systemic immunogenicity of LNP-mRNA (e.g., IFN-α, IL-6 levels) is not assessed, leaving the risk of TLR activation unresolved.
2. No Assessment of Hydrogel Degradation Kinetics
The degradation profile of the hydrogel is not characterized, making it impossible to determine whether GAS6 expression dynamics match material breakdown and mRNA release.
3. Lack of Appropriate Positive Controls
Key functional assays (macrophage M2 polarization, phagocytosis) do not include positive controls (e.g., IL-4), making the biological significance of the observed effects unclear.
4. Unresolved Mechanisms Involving TAM Receptors
The study confirms activation of the TAM family but does not dissect individual contributions (e.g., via Axl inhibitors or MerTK knockout). Functional mechanisms are speculative and unsupported by targeted experiments.
5. Limited Spatiotemporal Delivery Control
The hydrogel system appears to rely solely on passive diffusion, with no quantification of GAS6 distribution across dermal layers or validation of delivery to therapeutic targets.
6. No Active Targeting Strategy
Compared to current state-of-the-art delivery systems, the platform lacks ligand-mediated or inflammation-responsive targeting mechanisms. Transwell assays are insufficient to demonstrate effective LNP localization.
7. Hydrogel–LNP Interaction Unclear
The potential for the hydrogel to hinder or enhance LNP release is not assessed. No comparison is made to free LNP, making it impossible to determine whether the material system is synergistic or detrimental.
8. Lack of Environmental Responsiveness
The hydrogel has a fixed phase transition at 25°C and was only tested under physiological conditions. Its performance in pathophysiological environments (e.g., acidic or inflamed wounds) is unknown.
9. Mismatch Between Material and Biological Timelines
The release kinetics of GAS6 mRNA are not shown to align with the wound healing timeline. No data are provided on residual material or potential fibrotic responses due to prolonged retention.
Minor Concerns
1. Important physical properties of the hydrogel (e.g., pore size, network structure) are not reported.
2. The immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 4g is qualitative and lacks layer-specific quantification.
3. The manuscript would benefit from improved discussion on how this system compares to existing targeted delivery platforms in terms of precision, responsiveness, and translational potential.

Local assessment at injection sites showed no adverse effects on hair regeneration, follicular density, dermal thickness, or collagen volume fraction after 30 days (Supplementary Fig. 5a–f). Systemically, no gross or microscopic alterations were detected in major organs, and plasma inflammatory cytokine levels remained comparable to controls (Supplementary Fig. 5g–i). The hydrogel exhibited microenvironment-dependent degradation, with slow kinetics in PBS but accelerated breakdown in collagenase I, mimicking the proteolytic wound environment (Supplementary Fig. 4c). For the macrophage polarization and efferocytosis experiments, we introduced LNP-IL-4 mRNA as a positive control. The results confirmed that LNP-IL-4 mRNA promoted M2 polarization and enhanced efferocytosis, as expected (Fig. 3f–j). Notably, LNP-GAS6 mRNA demonstrated a stronger enhancement of efferocytosis than LNP-IL-4 mRNA (p<0.01; Fig. 3h–j), indicating that GAS6 signaling exerts immunomodulatory effects superior to those of a classical M2-polarizing stimulus. We agree that dissecting the individual contributions of TAM family members is crucial for understanding the signaling mechanisms through which GAS6 promotes regenerative healing. To delineate the specific contributions of TAM receptors, we inhibited AXL and MERTK signaling in murine acute wounds using Bemcentinib and UNC2025, respectively (Fig. 6a). Both inhibitors significantly impaired repair, delaying wound closure and exacerbating scar formation (Fig. 6b, c). Although attenuated, the therapeutic effect of LNP-GAS6 mRNA@Gel remained significant, indicating that it promoted repair even when individual TAM receptors were blocked (Fig. 6b, c). This functional compensation among TAM receptors not only helps coordinate the repair process, but also highlights the therapeutic advantage of using a broad-spectrum TAM ligand agonist (LNP-GAS6 mRNA@Gel) over receptor-specific targeting. We are grateful for this suggestion, which has substantially deepened our mechanistic inquiry.

5. Limited Spatiotemporal Delivery Control
The hydrogel system appears to rely solely on passive diffusion, with no quantification of GAS6 distribution across dermal layers or validation of delivery to therapeutic targets.
Response:
We agree that quantifying the distribution of GAS6 across wound layers is essential to validate our delivery strategy. While we have not performed direct co-localization staining for GAS6 and specific cell markers, our immunofluorescence analysis (as shown in Fig. 4g-i) quantitatively demonstrated that GAS6 expression was significantly higher in the deep dermis (particularly in the reticular dermis at both the wound center and edge), compared to superficial layers. This region-specific enrichment is functionally critical, as pathological scarring is primarily driven by dysregulated inflammation and fibrosis originating in the deep dermis.
These data provide clear evidence that our hydrogel system enables spatially restricted delivery of GAS6 mRNA to the therapeutically most relevant tissue layer. We believe the current layer-specific expression data, combined with the functional scar reduction outcomes across three animal models, strongly support the spatiotemporal delivery capability of our platform.

6. No Active Targeting Strategy
Compared to current state-of-the-art delivery systems, the platform lacks ligand-mediated or inflammation-responsive targeting mechanisms. Transwell assays are insufficient to demonstrate effective LNP localization.
Response:
Our delivery approach was deliberately designed based on the biological characteristics of GAS6 as a secreted protein that exerts its effects through paracrine signaling rather than requiring direct cell-specific internalization. While ligand-mediated targeting strategies are valuable for systemic delivery or specific cellular uptake, our localized hydrogel platform achieves effective spatial targeting through different mechanisms:
 Physical Confinement and Sustained Release: The thermosensitive hydrogel acts as a local reservoir that confines LNPs within the wound bed, preventing rapid clearance and ensuring prolonged GAS6 expression precisely where needed. Our in vivo imaging data (Fig. 4d-f) demonstrate significantly improved retention compared to free LNPs.
 Biological Targeting through Protein Secretion: Once translated from the delivered mRNA, GAS6 is secreted and naturally distributes within the wound microenvironment, activating TAM receptors on nearby macrophages. This avoids the complexity of engineering LNPs for specific cell targeting while still achieving the desired biological effect.
 Spatial Localization Evidence: Our immunofluorescence data (Fig. 4g-i) confirm that GAS6 protein is predominantly expressed in therapeutically relevant areas—specifically enriched in the deep dermis where pathological scarring originates.
We agree that inflammation-responsive elements could further enhance the system's sophistication. However, the current platform's simplicity (using clinically validated components without additional targeting ligand), may facilitate faster translational development while effectively addressing the clinical need for localized scar prevention.

Our comparative studies clearly demonstrate that the hydrogel does not hinder but significantly enhances the overall performance of LNPs in the dynamic wound environment. Direct comparison between free LNP and hydrogel-formulated LNP reveals several key advantages:
 Enhanced Retention and Stability: Free LNP injections suffered from substantial wound leakage, resulting in weak and variable fluorescence signals (Fig. 4d-f). In contrast, the hydrogel acts as a protective reservoir that firmly retains LNPs at the target site, ensuring sustained local presence.
 Improved Distribution Kinetics: Additional imaging at 6 and 12 hours (now in Fig. 4d-f) shows that while free LNPs exhibited uneven distribution and rapid clearance, the hydrogel formulation achieved earlier, more intense, and more uniform signal distribution throughout the wound bed.
 Optimized Release Profile: The hydrogel enables a controlled release kinetics that aligns perfectly with the therapeutic window. Rather than impeding LNP function, the hydrogel maintains LNPs in the wound microenvironment, facilitating prolonged and robust protein production that free LNPs cannot achieve.
The superior and sustained fluorescence signal in the hydrogel group, coupled with the poor performance of free LNPs, provides compelling evidence that the hydrogel-LNP combination acts synergistically rather than detrimentally. This protective, sustained-release mechanism is particularly crucial in the dynamic and exudative environment of acute wounds. We appreciate the opportunity to clarify this point and have strengthened the corresponding results section to better highlight these comparative advantages.

The hydrogel has a fixed phase transition at 25°C and was only tested under physiological conditions. Its performance in pathophysiological environments (e.g., acidic or inflamed wounds) is unknown.

We have conducted additional experiments to evaluate its performance under pathophysiological conditions. As shown in Fig. 4a–b, our thermosensitive PLGA-PEG-PLGA hydrogel exhibits a reversible sol-gel transition at ~25°C, enabling rapid gelation within 15 seconds upon application to both acute and diabetic wounds. Most importantly, we observed no significant delay in gelation kinetics even in the hyperglycemic and inflammatory microenvironment of diabetic wounds, confirming the robustness of its temperature-dependent behavior.
While the current system relies primarily on thermos-sensitivity rather than pH or enzyme-mediated responsiveness, its rapid gelation and physical stability under pathophysiological conditions ensure reliable retention and localized delivery of GAS6 mRNA within the wound bed. We appreciate this valuable feedback, which helps highlight the current robustness for our platform.

Early inflammatory events (particularly within the first 72 hours), are decisive in determining regenerative versus fibrotic outcomes. Our transcriptomic data (both bulk and single-cell) confirm that endogenous GAS6 is downregulated during early inflammation, and that inflammatory priming of dermal fibroblasts is a pivotal driver of scarring (Fig. 1a-l). To reverse this deficit, our LNP-GAS6 mRNA@Gel system was engineered to achieve peak GAS6 protein expression on post-operative day 3 (463.75 ± 80.17 pg/mg tissue), followed by a gradual decline (Supplementary Fig. 4g). In vivo degradation tracking confirmed near-complete hydrogel elimination within 72 hours post-application (Supplementary Fig. 4e, f), demonstrating favorable clearance kinetics that preclude long-term material retention. Regarding potential fibrotic responses due to material retention, local assessment at injection sites showed no adverse effects on hair regeneration, follicular density, dermal thickness, or collagen volume fraction after 30 days (Supplementary Fig. 5a–f). Systemically, no gross or microscopic alterations were detected in major organs, and plasma inflammatory cytokine levels remained comparable to controls (Supplementary Fig. 5g–i). These data collectively demonstrate that LNP-GAS6 mRNA@Gel is well-tolerated both locally and systemically.
Together, these results demonstrate that our delivery system achieves biologically relevant kinetics without eliciting adverse fibrotic responses, supporting its therapeutic safety and temporal compatibility with the wound healing process.
